clinicalPearls: A congenital anterior diaphragmatic hernia through the retrosternal foramen of Morgagni, usually on the right side
The least common type of congenital diaphragmatic hernia and often presents late in adulthood, frequently as an incidental finding
May contain omentum, transverse colon, stomach, or liver within a peritoneal sac
Appears on a chest radiograph as a well-defined right cardiophrenic angle mass or opacity
CT confirms the diagnosis by showing herniated abdominal contents, often with a characteristic band of omental fat and vessels crossing the defect
Symptoms, when present, include vague chest or upper abdominal discomfort, cough, or gastrointestinal symptoms from herniated bowel
Surgical repair is generally recommended even when asymptomatic because of the risk of incarceration or strangulation of contents
reference.pathophysiology: The foramen of Morgagni is a small anterior triangular gap between the sternal and costal muscular origins of the diaphragm, where the superior epigastric vessels pass. A congenital weakness or failure of muscular fusion at this point leaves a retrosternal defect through which abdominal contents, carried within a peritoneal sac, can herniate into the thorax. Raised intra-abdominal pressure from obesity, pregnancy, constipation, or exertion promotes progressive herniation, which is why many cases only become apparent in adult life. Herniated omentum or bowel is usually asymptomatic but can become obstructed, incarcerated, or strangulated.
additionalDifferentials: Anterior mediastinal mass or thymic lesion
Lung or pleural-based mass at the cardiophrenic angle
additionalInvestigations: Chest radiograph showing a right cardiophrenic angle opacity
Contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax and abdomen to confirm herniated contents and the fatty band sign
Contrast studies of the gastrointestinal tract when bowel is thought to be involved
MRI in selected cases to characterise soft-tissue contents
Assessment for associated congenital anomalies in younger patients
redFlags: Acute obstruction, incarceration, or strangulation of herniated bowel with pain and vomiting
Signs of ischaemia of herniated contents
Respiratory compromise from a large hernia
Rapidly increasing size of a cardiophrenic mass
reference.prognosis: The outlook after elective repair is excellent with low recurrence, whereas emergency presentation with incarceration or strangulation carries higher morbidity, which is the rationale for repairing even asymptomatic hernias.
pitfalls: Mistaking the hernia for a benign pericardial fat pad or cyst and leaving it unassessed
Failing to recognise herniated bowel at risk of obstruction
Overlooking the diagnosis on a plain radiograph and attributing the opacity to a mediastinal mass
Underestimating the risk of complications when advising conservative management
references: Murray & Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine
management: Surgical repair is the definitive treatment and is generally recommended even when asymptomatic because of the risk of obstruction and strangulation, comprising reduction of contents, excision of the peritoneal sac and closure of the retrosternal defect by an open or minimally invasive laparoscopic or thoracoscopic approach, with mesh reinforcement for large defects
Emergency surgery for incarceration, strangulation or bowel obstruction
Preoperative confirmation and operative planning with contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax and abdomen
Assess for associated congenital anomalies in paediatric presentations
Perioperative supportive care with postoperative follow-up to detect the uncommon recurrence
